It turns out the advancements we’re getting in coding and computer use, combined with industry specific understand and general reasoning, can bring automation to a large number of areas of knowledge work.

We’re entering the era of autonomous collaborators in a number of industries that haven’t yet had their claude code or codex moment yet. But now this is going to happen. 

We’ll see it in animation, film production, gaming, manufacturing, architecture, product design, robotics, and more. All of these fields have the potential of driving far more output similar to what we’ve seen in software engineering. There’s no inherent finite demand for these categories of work.

“Software is eating the world” is finally in a much bigger way happening because of AI.

Agent swarms have the potential to drive yet another leap in output from AI. The impact will be a clear separation between teams that adopt this pattern of work and those that don’t. 

The progression has roughly been: chat gave us quick turn AI responses that let us work a bit faster, but we were still rate limited by our interactions; then agents that can go off and complete entire tasks for us, accelerating hours or days of work into minutes; to now swarms of agents that are goal seeking and will find any route to the successful completion of a project, where there’s no inherent limit to the productivity gains. 

We can imagine a future where, for any task in which value can be created within a self-contained digital environment, swarms will be able to complete the work faster than any other approach.

Essentially any area where value creation is currently bound by the amount of research you can do, the amount of decisions made with a set of software tools, the amount of data processed or consumed, and the amount of code (or code adjacent) that can be generated. 

This means swarms will play a big role in game development, coding, trading, life sciences research, IT automation, cyber, math breakthroughs, animation, and plenty of other areas of work that have these characteristics. 

There’s a lot of opportunity to build the harnesses, applied AI products, and infrastructure for how these agents operate. And most importantly there’s a ton of opportunity for those that can wire up work in this way. It’s going to be an entire new field of FDE work available.

Agents are going to work with enterprise files 100X more than people do today. This is why we're excited to partner with Anthropic to bring full read/write interoperability to Box content via Claude.

Now you can have an agent not only pull up content to work with in a workflow, but also write back file updates to Box and view them directly inside of Claude, all via MCP. You can create, edit, and update contracts, presentations, strategy docs, and any other content.

When we started Box we couldn't have imagined all the ways that we'd be working with our unstructured data in the future, but it's clear that agents and people will be producing vastly more artifacts than we imagined. We're building the platform that makes it incredibly seamless and secure to work with your content from any agent.

Google has released its first decision model, Gemini Decision 1, scoring 66 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index and leading in knowledge and reasoning benchmarks

Gemini Decision 1 from @GoogleDeepMind scores 66 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1, in line with Elephant 9B (@baselabs) and Jev 1.14 (@typesafeai), and 7 points behind leaders Drex Max v1.1 (@NaceAI) and GLiDE v1.2 (@fastinoAI), which both score 73. It is priced at $0.10 per 1M input tokens and costs $345 per 1M Tasks across the Index, around three times higher than Drex Max v1.1 ($103) due to its higher pricing

Key results for Gemini Decision 1:

➤ Not yet frontier on Decision Index: Gemini Decision 1 scores 66 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index. It leads knowledge and reasoning benchmarks, scoring 66 on AA-Omniscience-Decision and 49 on HLE-MultiChoice. It trails on other evaluations, including our new proprietary classification and extraction benchmark AA-Paperclip, where it answers all 15 questions correctly on 33% of documents vs. 63% for Drex Max v1.1

➤ More than 3x the Cost per Task of leading models: Gemini Decision 1 costs $345 per 1M Tasks, compared with $103 for Drex Max v1.1, $156 for Jev 1.14. This difference is driven by its token price of $0.10 per 1M input tokens vs. $0.03 for Drex Max v1.1. Gemini Decision 1 has a similar Cost per 1M Tasks to GPT-6 Luna (Decisions, $339)

➤ Strong calibration for reasoning tasks: We measure calibration with the Brier score, the average squared gap between the probability a model assigns to its chosen answer and whether that answer was correct (lower is better). Gemini Decision 1 has a Brier score of 0.18 across the Index, between Drex Max v1.1 (0.16) and Jev 1.14 (0.19). Calibration varies by task. with its Brier score of 0.20 on HLE-MultiChoice among the lowest of all models in the Index, while its 0.14 on When2Call compares with 0.04 for Drex Max v1.1

overheard from friends talking about AI in China, and it’s very alarming

- AI short films went massive in China market because of how good the video models are now

- the first wave of people who mastered using AI to generate short films and comics made quite some money because they could produce a lot more content than traditional workflows

- but within just a few months, everybody and their mom could make equally good short films because all the expertise could be written in a markdown file

- when everyone’s more productive, no one actually has an advantage and it’s a race to the bottom. very quickly it became impossible to make money, and everyone’s busier than they were without AI

- the only one making money now is companies like bytedance who owns user demand and distribution. they sell ads to creators who pay to get traffic, and eventually ad spend became 80% of those creators’ operating expense, while AI tokens is less than 5%

so what are the problems here? 

1. there’s no moat if you are creating anything with AI

if a human is really good at something, and it’s hard to find more humans who can do the same, they can leverage the scarcity of their skill to get paid very well

but if AI is good at something, it will be infinitely replicated, so there’s no scarcity hence you can’t really expect a sustainable business by creating anything with AI

2. more creators created more content people actually liked. that’s a good thing

but the economical benefit of that all got absorbed by the distribution platforms

there’s a famous chinese poem 遍身罗绮者，不是养蚕人 - it basically says people who dress well aren’t the people making dresses. that’s exactly what’s happening here

if our society doesn’t figure out a better way to distribute wealth, AI will help billionaires become trillionaires while average people become more exhausted than ever

Currently working towards a bigger open LLM roundup. But in the meantime, just one of the interesting trends that stood out. I.e., looks like the transition from full to hybrid attention continues.

In 2025, there were still lots of full attention models, with a shift to "some full attention" hybrids.

In the first half of 2026, the trend towards "some full attention" hybrids continued.

And now, in the second half of 2026, we have a 50/50 split between "some full attention" hybrids and models that don't use full attention at all anymore. And yes, there are also no full attention models anymore. 

The plot legend here means,

- Full attention throughout = Global MHA, GQA, dense MLA, CCA in EVERY layer. 
- Some full attention = Full global attn mixed with: sliding-window/chunked attention, Gated DeltaNet, KDA, Mamba-2, Lightning Attention, convolutions, sparse attention. 
- No full attention = Zero dense global layers.

The main implication is that the trend goes towards making long contexts cheaper to use. This means, it makes the architectures more suitable for long documents and conversations, large code bases, and of course agent usecases that rely on a lot of tool calls.

In particular, there are two distinct efficiency gains here:

1) Less attention computation, since sparse attention and the like select tokens or blocks from the context and performs the expensive attention operation from only that subset. (Note that it can still retrieve information from distant positions.)

2) Less memory for retaining context in some architectures, meaning that recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet maintain a fixed-size state. Of course, this saves memory, but compressing the history creates challenges for exact retrieval, so they are usually intermixed with traditional attention methods (sparse or full).
